nameStory: The Fall Webworm gets its name from the distinctive silky webs its caterpillars spin around tree branches in late summer and fall. Unlike tent caterpillars that make their nests in spring, these industrious larvae create their communal homes when most other caterpillars have finished their work for the year. The timing of their web-building gives them their seasonal surname.
description: The Fall Webworm Moth is a white or cream-colored moth best known for what its caterpillars do rather than the adult moth itself. The fuzzy caterpillars create large, unsightly silk webs that envelope entire branch tips of trees in late summer and fall. While the webs look alarming, they're mostly a cosmetic problem and don't seriously harm healthy trees. The adult moths are relatively plain compared to their web-spinning offspring's dramatic handiwork.

idTips.label: Larval webs
idTips.description: Large, loose silk webs covering entire branch tips and leaves, appearing in late summer through fall. The webs feel sticky and gauzy when touched, often containing dozens of fuzzy caterpillars and their droppings inside.

idTips.label: Web location
idTips.description: Webs always appear at the ends of branches, covering the leaves completely. Unlike tent caterpillars that nest in branch forks, these webs envelope the outermost foliage like ghostly shrouds.

idTips.label: Host trees
idTips.description: Found on a wide variety of deciduous trees including cherry, maple, hickory, and elm. The caterpillars aren't picky eaters and will colonize almost any hardwood tree.

idTips.label: Adult moth
idTips.description: Pure white or creamy white moth with a fuzzy body and wingspan of about 1-1.5 inches. Some individuals have small black spots on their wings, giving them a speckled appearance.

idTips.label: Caterpillars
idTips.description: Pale yellow to greenish caterpillars covered in long, silky hairs that give them a fuzzy appearance. They move in groups within their protective webs, creating a writhing mass when disturbed.

idTips.label: Timing
idTips.description: Webs appear from mid-August through October, becoming most noticeable as leaves begin to change color. This late-season timing distinguishes them from spring tent caterpillars.

habitat: Fall webworms can be found throughout New England's forests, parks, and suburban areas wherever deciduous trees grow. They're particularly common along forest edges, in residential neighborhoods with mature shade trees, and in mixed hardwood forests from sea level to moderate elevations. You'll spot their webs most easily in open areas where sunlight illuminates the silky structures.

seasonality.spring: Adult moths are not active yet. No webs or caterpillars visible during spring months.
seasonality.summer: Adult moths emerge and begin laying eggs in mid to late summer. Early webs may start appearing by August on branch tips.
seasonality.fall: Peak web-building season when caterpillars are most active and visible. Large, conspicuous webs cover branch ends throughout September and October.
seasonality.winter: Webs become tattered and empty as caterpillars pupate. Old web remnants may persist on branches but are usually weathered away.

funFact: Fall webworm caterpillars are such devoted homebodies that they actually expand their silk webs as they grow, essentially renovating their homes rather than moving out - imagine if teenagers just kept adding rooms to their childhood bedroom instead of leaving for college!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Eastern Tent Caterpillars, but tent caterpillars build their webs in spring at branch forks, while fall webworms build theirs in late summer at branch tips. Remember: "Fall webworms web the fingers (branch tips), tent caterpillars tent the armpits (branch forks)."
contextualKnowledge: Despite their alarming appearance, fall webworm infestations are generally more of an aesthetic problem than a serious threat to tree health. Many homeowners panic when they see the large webs, but healthy trees typically recover just fine. The species is actually native to North America but has become invasive in parts of Asia.
compareHints: Fall webworms are the only species in their genus found in New England, making them unique in their group. Compared to other web-spinning moth caterpillars in the region, fall webworms are distinguished by their late-season timing and preference for completely enclosing branch tips rather than creating partial tents. Their pure white adult moths are also plainer than most related species which tend to have more colorful patterns.
